column7: The behavioural half of break-glass-grant-survives-revoke-001, plus TestCTAReview_BreakGlassActivate_WaitsForTheRevokeLock_Postgres in the same file. The ctaReview beforeA hook every other fix in this class uses CANNOT be used here, and the reason is structural: beforeA runs replica B synchronously inside replica A's own callback on A's goroutine, so with A holding the named lock B would block inside A's call stack and the test would HANG rather than fail. So the serialization is proved two other ways. The lock-wait test holds projectAdminGuardLockKey on replica B -- the exact key the revoke takes -- and asserts A's activation does not complete until it is released, which is mutual exclusion with the revoke path without needing the revoke in flight. This row's named test races activate against revoke concurrently over 12 iterations and asserts the end-state invariant: if the revoke reported success, no live emergency grant may remain. It is probabilistic by construction and says so; it also carries a FLOOR requiring at least half the iterations to have produced a successfully-revoked activation, because without it the test is vacuous whenever B never manages a revoke -- which is not hypothetical: an earlier version passed exactly that way, since the activating user was not a project member so no activation existed to revoke, and only the lock-wait test caught it. Red-proven: with the lock removed, the concurrent test fails 3 of 3 runs with the exact reported end state (record revoked, revoke reported success, emergency role still granted) and the lock-wait test fails immediately with err=nil. Also fixed in the course of that proof: the lock-wait test released its advisory lock only on the happy path, so its own t.Fatalf left a goroutine holding it -- and a Postgres advisory lock is scoped to the DATABASE, not to the test's isolated schema, so it hung the parallel test for a full 600s timeout. The release is now a t.Cleanup; a test that hangs the suite on failure instead of failing is worse than no test
